edition: Newton, Principia, Andrew Motte trans., 1729 (Wikisource); Book I, Section I (Lemma XII cited later in Prop. XI); Plate 4, Fig. 1.

figures.caption: All parallelograms described about conjugate diameters of a given ellipse or hyperbola are equal to one another.

text.latex: Here is a single \textcolor{ellblue}{ellipse} with centre $O$, drawn wider than tall. Through the centre run two \textcolor{conjorange}{conjugate diameters} $PQ$ and $RS$ --- note that they are \emph{skewed}, not perpendicular, for that is the whole point of the lemma. About the ellipse is described the \textcolor{pargreen}{parallelogram} whose four sides are tangent to the curve exactly at the four diameter endpoints $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$. Apollonius proved that no matter which pair of conjugate diameters one chooses, the circumscribed parallelogram always has the very same area, namely $4ab$, where $a$ and $b$ are the semi-axes of the ellipse. Newton invokes this fact without proof, remarking only: \textit{This is demonstrated by the writers on the conic sections.}
